label: Density Control and Local Regularity
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 505 through 524, asks how the density of a displacement interpolant behaves at intermediate times. The recurring theme is that upper bounds on the endpoint densities propagate inward along the geodesic, so mass never piles up partway through the interpolation, and this control is the gateway to local regularity.

label: The Displacement Interpolant
notes: We fix the Wasserstein geodesic joining two measures and push the optimal map forward by a fraction of the displacement. The interpolant inherits its mass from the endpoints through a single optimal coupling, so understanding its density reduces to understanding how the interpolating map distorts volume at each time.

label: Why Density Can Blow Up
notes: Without curvature or convexity control, trajectories can focus toward a common region and the Jacobian of the interpolation map can collapse, sending density to infinity. The danger is geometric: geodesics that contract too sharply concentrate mass, so we must quantify how much the interpolation Jacobian is allowed to shrink.

label: The Jacobian of Interpolation
notes: The density of the interpolant is the endpoint density divided by the Jacobian determinant of the interpolation map. Controlling density therefore means bounding this Jacobian away from zero, and the Jacobian factorizes through the geodesic, exposing the role of volume distortion coefficients along each transport path.

label: Distortion Coefficients
notes: The volume distortion coefficients measure how a Riemannian geodesic spreads or contracts an infinitesimal bundle of transport rays. Under a lower Ricci bound these coefficients obey explicit comparison estimates, and substituting them into the Jacobian formula converts an abstract curvature hypothesis into a concrete pointwise density inequality.

label: The Density Bound
notes: Putting the pieces together yields the central estimate: the interpolant density at any intermediate time is bounded by a curvature-dependent multiple of the larger endpoint density. The bound is uniform in time, so the entire geodesic family lives below a single ceiling determined only by the endpoints and the lower curvature bound.

label: No Mass Concentration
notes: The uniform ceiling means no intermediate measure can develop a spike: every interpolant remains absolutely continuous with a controlled essential supremum. Mass that started spread out stays spread out, which rules out the formation of atoms or unbounded densities partway along the displacement path.

label: Local Regularity
notes: Once densities are uniformly bounded, the interpolation maps gain quantitative regularity on compact sets. The transport rays do not cross, velocities stay locally bounded, and the family of maps becomes equicontinuous, so one can pass to limits and differentiate along the geodesic without losing control of the geometry.

label: Equicontinuity of the Family
notes: Uniform density and Jacobian bounds give a modulus of continuity that does not depend on the time parameter. By Arzela-Ascoli the interpolation maps form a compact equicontinuous family, so limits of approximating geodesics are again geodesics and the structure survives the limiting process intact.

label: Feeding Displacement Convexity
notes: Displacement-convexity arguments evaluate functionals such as entropy along the geodesic, and those evaluations require the interpolant to have a genuine, integrable density. The bounds of this chapter supply exactly that input, making the second-derivative computations of the convexity machinery well defined and rigorous.

label: Well-Posedness Payoff
notes: With density control in hand, the convexity inequalities driving functional inequalities and stability estimates become legitimate. The chapter therefore acts as the analytic foundation beneath the geometric story: bounded interpolation densities are the hypothesis that lets the entire displacement-convexity program run without gaps.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We saw that endpoint density bounds, refracted through Jacobian and distortion estimates under a lower curvature bound, control the interpolant density at every intermediate time. This prevents concentration, yields local regularity and equicontinuity, and certifies the displacement-convexity computations used throughout the later theory.
